texto: I'd been driving for almost 11 hours when the
detour signs pushed me off the interstate.
The road narrowed to two lanes, the radio lost its station, and for a long time the
only light out there was my own headlights.
Around two in the morning I saw a gas station sign glowing over the fields.
The pumps were on, the store was dark, and there was one other car parked by the air
machine with its engine running and nobody inside.
This was six years ago, in October.
I was 24 and moving back home to Missouri after
a job in Colorado fell apart, with everything
I owned in the backseat of a Corolla with a cracked windshield.
I kept telling myself one more hour, and by the
time the detour came up, I was too tired
to be smart about it.
For a while there was a pickup truck ahead of
me, the only other headlights for miles.
At a crossroads with no signs at all, it turned
onto a dirt road, and its lights went out
almost at once.
It didn't park, it didn't slow down that I could
see, the lights just went out, and the
dark closed over the spot where it had been.
I kept going straight, because the orange arrows told me to.
I pulled up to the pump farthest from the other car.
It was an old station wagon, dark green with wood panels on the sides.
Exhaust was rising from it in the cold.
The headlights were off, but the dome light was
on, and I could see a jacket on the passenger
seat and a fast food bag on the dashboard.
In the back, there was a child's booster seat,
and a stuffed rabbit sitting in it, turned
around so it faced the rear window.
Two small sneakers sat on the floor mat underneath,
side by side, like someone had taken them
off and meant to put them right back on.
I filled the tank and waited.
I think I wanted to see someone walk back to that car, just so I could stop thinking
about it.
Nobody came.
The engine kept idling, steady, like it had been running for hours.
Then, while I was watching, the dome light went off.
I stood there with the nozzle in my hand and stared at the dark windows.
A few seconds later, it came back on.
Nobody had opened a door.
I hung up the nozzle, got back in my car, and left.
At the edge of the lot, I looked in the rearview mirror one last time.
The dome light was still on.
The stuffed rabbit was facing forward now.
About twenty minutes later, the detour signs ended at a truck stop.
The first real building I'd seen in hours.
The diner, a couple of semis parked out back with
their running lights on, and a sign that
said Open 24 hours, with two of the letters burned out.
I parked by the entrance because I needed coffee, and I needed to be around people.
Inside it was warm and smelled like burnt coffee and bacon grease.
There was a trucker at the counter, reading
his phone, an old man asleep in a booth by
the window, and one waitress.
Her name tag said D.
She called me honey before I'd even sat down.
I took a booth facing the door and ordered coffee and a slice of pie.
That's when the couple came in.
They were young.
Maybe my age.
He wore a gray hoodie, and she had on a denim
jacket that was too thin for the weather.
It had started to rain, and the shoulders of both jackets were dark with it.
They were arguing in that low, tight way people argue in public.
As they passed my booth, the girl said, every single time, Ray, every single time.
He didn't answer.
They sat two booths down from me, across the aisle,
and D. brought them menus and two waters.
I ate my pie and heard pieces of their conversation,
something about a wrong turn and whose idea
it was to leave so late.
At one point, Ray said, we'll be fine, we're almost there.
She didn't say anything back.
When D. refilled my coffee, she asked where I was headed.
I said Missouri.
She glanced out the window and lowered her voice.
When you leave, honey, follow the signs back to the interstate.
Don't take the old county road, even if your phone says it's shorter.
I asked her why.
She smiled, said that road wasn't kept up anymore, and walked away.
I got up to use the restroom, at the end of a
short hallway past the kitchen, where one
of the lights kept flickering.
I was washing my hands when I heard her voice through
the wall, from outside, from the parking
lot, every single time, Ray.
It was the same tired, angry tone and the same words.
I turned off the water and listened.
A man's voice answered her, too low to make out,
and then a car door shut, then nothing.
I stood there with my wet hands out in front of
me, telling myself there was a window open
somewhere that sound carries.
When I came out and walked back toward my booth, the bell over the front door rang.
It was them.
Gray hoodie, thin denim jacket, both of them dark with rain.
They walked in the same way, him a step ahead,
her behind with her arms crossed, and as they
passed me, she said, every single time, Ray, every single time.
I stopped in the aisle and looked at the booth where they'd been sitting.
It was empty.
No menus, no glasses, no wet rings on the table.
It had been wiped down like nobody had used it all night.
They sat in that same booth.
Dee came over with two menus and two waters,
smiled at them, and said, evening you two.
Rough night out there?
The way you'd greet someone who just walked in.
I made myself walk past their table on the way back to mine.
Up close, I could see the rain on her jacket,
soaked into the denim in exactly the same
shape as before.
Ray had his wrist on the table, and his watch caught the light.
It was an old digital watch.
It read 214, and the whole time I stood there, it didn't change.
I sat down, and I watched them have the same
conversation, wrong turn, leaving too late.
The trucker never looked up from his phone, and
the old man by the window never woke up.
Nobody else in that room seemed to think anything was wrong.
I still don't know where the nerve came from,
but I walked over and stood at the end of
their table.
I asked, as normally as I could, if they'd just gotten there.
The girl kept staring out at the parking lot.
Ray looked up at me.
His eyes were red, like he hadn't slept in a very long time.
Then he said, very calmly, we'll be fine.
We're almost there.
He said it to me, exactly the way he'd said it to her.
Then Dee was beside me with the coffee pot.
She put her hand on my arm, very gently, and walked
me back to my booth like I was a little
kid who'd wandered off in a store.
Don't bother them, honey, she said quietly.
They never stay long.
She filled my cup to the top.
I hadn't touched it since the last time she filled it.
I left a twenty on the table and walked out.
Outside the rain had stopped, and the parking lot was dry.
Completely dry.
No puddles, no drops on my windshield.
I locked myself in my car and sat there with the
engine running until the sky turned gray,
and then I followed the signs back to the interstate,
exactly the way Dee told me to.
I didn't pass the gas station on the way back.
I took the same road, I'm sure of that.
It just wasn't there anymore.
I had a cheap dash cam back then, the kind that records over itself every few hours.
When I got home and checked it, most of that night was gone.
The only file left starts as I pull into the truck stop at 2.14 in the morning.
I park, the camera keeps recording, and about
a minute later, the dark green station wagon
pulls into the spot right in front of me.
Engine running, dome light on, nobody inside.
The date on that clip is October 14th.
The year is the one before I ever drove that road.
I still drive that interstate a couple of times a year.
When the detour signs are up, I don't take them.
I stop in the last town before the exit, park somewhere
well lit, and sleep in my car until
morning.
